items.title: SBI Data Breach Claim – Hackers Allegedly Claim Access to 3.75 Lakh Users’ Database
items.summary: An unverified SBI data breach claim alleges that a threat actor named Siriusim posted customer records and banking documents online. The claimed dataset contains 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files, but those figures do not establish that 3.75 lakh unique customers were affected. CyberPulse reported the allegation on October 16, 2026. Its post described personal customer information, loan applications, supporting documents, account-opening forms and address details. The actor called it the first disclosure of the dataset. The authenticity, source and extent of the alleged exposure remain unverified. SBI Data Breach Claim According to India Today , Siriusim posted the claim on BreachForums and shared what it described as four sample customer records. The report said the material may include Know Your Customer (KYC) records, Aadhaar numbers and residential addresses. These details remain allegations rather than confirmed findings from an investigation. CSV files store information in rows and columns, while PDFs can hold forms and scanned documents. A row count alone cannot show how many people appear in a dataset. Multiple applications or duplicate entries could relate to the same person, and document totals do not prove separate victims. India Today reported on October 19 that SBI had not addressed the claims when its article was published. The outlet said it had requested comment and could not independently confirm the breach. It also remained unclear whether the material was newly exposed or recycled from earlier leaks. The available reports do not establish how the alleged records were obtained. Their source could not be traced to SBI itself, a subsidiary or a service provider handling banking applications. There is no verified evidence in these reports identifying an exploited flaw, stolen login or compromised server. That uncertainty matters because documents bearing a bank’s name do not, by themselves, establish access to its core banking systems. Any investigation would need to validate samples, identify their owner, and check the claimed records against system logs before drawing conclusions about the source or scale. If genuine, the records could support identity theft, loan fraud and targeted phishing. Criminals could use application details to make fake bank calls or messages sound convincing. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake SBI reward apps and fraudulent YONO deactivation alerts , both relevant examples of banking impersonation, not evidence connecting those campaigns to this claim. An unverified SBI data breach claim alleges that a threat actor named Siriusim posted customer records and banking documents online. The claimed dataset contains 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files, but those figures do not establish that 3.75 lakh unique customers were affected.

CyberPulse reported the allegation on October 16, 2026. Its post described personal customer information, loan applications, supporting documents, account-opening forms and address details. The actor called it the first disclosure of the dataset. The authenticity, source and extent of the alleged exposure remain unverified.

SBI Data Breach Claim

According to India Today, Siriusim posted the claim on BreachForums and shared what it described as four sample customer records. The report said the material may include Know Your Customer (KYC) records, Aadhaar numbers and residential addresses. These details remain allegations rather than confirmed findings from an investigation.

CSV files store information in rows and columns, while PDFs can hold forms and scanned documents. A row count alone cannot show how many people appear in a dataset. Multiple applications or duplicate entries could relate to the same person, and document totals do not prove separate victims.

India Today reported on October 19 that SBI had not addressed the claims when its article was published. The outlet said it had requested comment and could not independently confirm the breach. It also remained unclear whether the material was newly exposed or recycled from earlier leaks.

The available reports do not establish how the alleged records were obtained. Their source could not be traced to SBI itself, a subsidiary or a service provider handling banking applications. There is no verified evidence in these reports identifying an exploited flaw, stolen login or compromised server.

That uncertainty matters because documents bearing a bank’s name do not, by themselves, establish access to its core banking systems. Any investigation would need to validate samples, identify their owner, and check the claimed records against system logs before drawing conclusions about the source or scale.

If genuine, the records could support identity theft, loan fraud and targeted phishing. Criminals could use application details to make fake bank calls or messages sound convincing. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake SBI reward apps and fraudulent YONO deactivation alerts, both relevant examples of banking impersonation, not evidence connecting those campaigns to this claim.

Customers should verify unexpected bank messages through official channels, avoid shared APK files, and never disclose passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords. SBI should assess the claim, preserve logs, and notify affected customers if an investigation confirms exposure. Until then, this remains an alleged data leak, not a confirmed compromise of accounts.

items.title: One Hacker Uses AI Agents to Breach Over 100 Company Websites for Just $5,000
items.summary: A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites while spending an estimated $5,000 on AI tokens, according to a Reuters investigation in October. The operation shows how one person can direct software to carry out complex attacks with little ongoing human input. The targets included sites linked to Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, although the reported impact differed across those companies. After the campaign began on September 25, the agents attempted to compromise more than 1,200 websites, mainly online stores in the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at NorForge, uncovered the activity while searching for exposed Cairn installations, an open-source platform that coordinates AI agents. Around October 2, he found roughly two dozen installations apparently being used for malicious activity. How Cairn Automated the Attacks Cairn is a general-purpose problem-solving engine rather than a tool built only for hacking. In the attacks described in NorForge’s technical report , operators supplied a target and a goal, then agents searched for weaknesses and worked toward gaining access. The platform stores findings on a shared project board so its agents can use earlier discoveries to choose their next steps. That allows them to try different paths when an initial approach fails, instead of relying on a single fixed scan. NorForge tracked the largest Chinese-language activity cluster as AIA0001, linking it to 14 dashboards containing more than 1,100 attack projects. Its target pipeline used Microsoft’s Playwright browser automation tool to check that shopping sites could accept orders before passing them to Cairn. The task instructions focused on finding ways to run code without signing in, including SQL injection, unsafe file uploads, login bypasses and unsafe handling of stored objects. The apparent aim was lasting access to shopping and payment systems that could later generate money. NorForge confirmed one claimed breach by checking a reported address on a hardware vendor’s website and finding a live uploader webshell. This server-side script allowed files to be placed on the compromised site, creating a foothold for further attacks. According to the agent’s own account, that attack combined unauthorized write access to a memcached session store with unsafe PHP object deserialization and older Zend Framework components. The chain turned weaknesses in session storage and object processing into server access, rather than depending on one obvious entry point. In another case, agents moved beyond a company’s main application after failing to find a weakness. They searched related infrastructure, found an exposed control panel, and spent hours testing its handling of data before reporting that they could run commands on the server. Low Costs, Long Running Agents Successful AIA0001 projects took just under 23 hours on average, while one ran for more than five days. Across the observed campaigns, NorForge estimated success at around 10%, although goals and targets varied between operators. Fagerland estimated the main campaign consumed about $5,000 in tokens, or roughly $50 per successful intrusion. These figures are estimates, not confirmed billing records. NorForge separately put the average task cost near $5 when failed and early-ending attempts were included, warning that uncertainty was substantial. Worker names suggested a Claude Code setup using a DeepSeek model, but NorForge did not confirm the full model configuration. Chinese-language instructions also do not establish the operator’s nationality, and researchers found no obvious state-backed activity in the exposed panels. Related reporting on AI agents used to steal retail credit card data described a separate campaign involving Cairn and other tools. Another investigation into DeepSeek-powered credential theft showed attackers using agents to exploit exposed secrets and weak settings, rather than relying on new flaws. Deere told Reuters it took corrective action and found no indication that attackers accessed sensitive information. SharkNinja said the affected system was a separate product support site and that the threat had been contained. Cummins was investigating a possible attack on a third-party-run website. Reuters could not determine how much data, if any, was taken across the breaches. NorForge also found hundreds of exposed secrets in the open panels and said it was working with Reuters to notify victims. The exposure also affected legitimate security testers. NorForge found unsecured testing dashboards revealing customer information, showing that poorly protected AI tools create risk during authorized work. Defenders should patch public-facing applications, restrict access to admin panels, and watch for unexpected files in web directories. Security teams should also review suspicious web requests and isolate servers where webshells are found, then investigate for stolen data, further access, and other malware before restoring service. items.title: Claude AI Detects Hidden Crypto Miner While Building Temperature Monitor App on Mac
items.summary: An ordinary coding task led to an unexpected security discovery when Claude Code reportedly found a hidden cryptocurrency miner on a developer’s Mac. The AI assistant was building a temperature monitoring app when unusually high sensor readings prompted it to investigate CPU activity. It identified XMRig consuming about 1,175% CPU, described as roughly 12 cores of processing load. The developer, posting as u/UntilHEX on Reddit , said Claude checked running processes after reviewing raw sensor data. The discovery offered an explanation for the Mac’s poor performance. However, the account remains a user report supported by a screenshot, rather than a published forensic investigation. High CPU Usage Exposed the Hidden Miner According to the shared screenshot, Claude reported that the CPU had peaked at 112°C. “Your Mac is running a cryptominer that I didn’t put there,” the assistant warned. Those figures reflect the reported session and have not been independently verified through hardware logs or a separate examination. The screenshot identified /tmp/rigupdater as the miner’s running location and pool.hashvault.sh as its mining pool destination. These details provide useful leads for investigators examining this specific device. They do not establish how the software arrived, who installed it, or whether other systems were affected. XMRig is not inherently malicious. It is mining software with official macOS builds, including support for Apple Silicon. The security concern is its apparent use without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Finding the program alone would not prove an infection without examining its installation, configuration, and activity. LaunchAgent Reportedly Kept the Miner Running Claude also flagged a suspicious property list file inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ . The screenshot described a randomly named startup entry dated August 29 that ran a large encoded script through bash , with KeepAlive enabled. Claude said the entry was already present before its development work began. Apple’s LaunchAgent documentation explains that user agents run within a logged-in user’s session. The KeepAlive setting can tell launchd to keep a job running. That makes the startup entry important because stopping a process without disabling its launcher may allow it to return. LaunchAgents themselves are legitimate macOS features, not automatic proof of malware. The screenshot also raised concern about credentials available on the Mac, including its GitHub login. That warning describes possible exposure, not confirmed theft. The public evidence does not show that passwords, access tokens, source code, or other files were stolen. The infection route and full scope remain unknown. Claude initially said it had not killed or removed anything. Instead, it requested permission to stop the startup item and miner, then move files into quarantine. UntilHEX later said the assistant performed cleanup, although one file required manual deletion because of an access issue. The behavior resembles techniques seen in other Mac threats, without proving a connection. Cyber Security News previously covered fake CAPTCHA attacks that install a backdoor and XMRig . That campaign used a LaunchAgent and could combine mining with password theft, showing why removing a miner alone may leave risks behind. Separate reporting on CrashStealer’s abuse of Apple crash-reporting branding also documented LaunchAgent persistence. Neither campaign has been linked to UntilHEX’s Mac. Their relevance is the shared use of trusted operating system features to keep unwanted software running. For affected users, the practical lesson is to investigate unexplained heat and sustained CPU load, review persistence, and check account exposure. Suspected compromise warrants isolation and password changes from a clean device. Claude’s discovery was useful, but the reported cleanup does not establish that every threat was removed.
